vulnerabilities.title: OOB_ARRAY_INDEX_MISSING_BOUNDS_CHECK

root_cause.description: In the 'Read Hash record' path of main, the user-supplied index read via scanf('%u') at 0x17d8 is used directly to access the hash_array at [rbp+rax*8-0x490] without any upper or lower bound check. The only validation performed is a NULL check on the dereferenced pointer value (test rax,rax at 0x17ed). The hash_array has only 16 valid entries (indices 0-15), but the unsigned index can be any value from 0 to 0xFFFFFFFF. The 'mov eax,eax' at 0x17e3 zero-extends the 32-bit unsigned value to 64-bit, so the index is treated as a large positive offset. For indices >= 16, the access reads beyond the hash_array into adjacent stack regions: the text buffer (idx 16-145), the stack canary (idx 145), the saved rbp (idx 146), the return address (idx 147), and potentially far beyond the stack frame for very large indices. If the OOB slot contains a non-NULL value, that value is then dereferenced as a pointer and 32 bytes are read and printed from it, creating an information disclosure primitive.

affected_objects: hash_array[16] at rbp-0x490 (stack pointer array, 0x80 bytes)

attack_surface.input: read_idx via scanf('%u') at address 0x17d8, stored at rbp-0x4b0
data_flow: scanf('%u', &read_idx) reads unsigned integer from stdin into rbp-0x4b0 at 0x17d8
mov eax, [rbp-0x4b0] loads the 32-bit unsigned index at 0x17dd
mov eax,eax zero-extends to 64-bit at 0x17e3 (unsigned, no sign extension)
mov rax, [rbp+rax*8-0x490] accesses hash_array[idx] with NO bounds check at 0x17e5
test rax,rax checks only if the loaded value is NULL at 0x17ed
If non-NULL: the loaded 8-byte value is treated as a pointer
Loop at 0x1829-0x186e: mov rdx, [rbp+rax*8-0x490] re-reads OOB slot, then add rax,rdx + movzx eax,[rax] dereferences the OOB pointer value, printing 32 bytes via printf('%02hhX')

security_check.expected: The read_idx should be validated to be within [0, 15] (the valid range of hash_array entries) before being used as an array index. An upper bound check (e.g., cmp idx, 0xf; ja abort) is required.
security_check.actual: No bounds check exists on read_idx. The only check is 'test rax,rax; jne' (NULL check) at 0x17ed-0x17f0, which only verifies the dereferenced pointer value is non-NULL. This check does not constrain the index at all — it merely filters out slots that happen to contain zero.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Missing upper bound check on the unsigned index before array access. The compute path correctly bounds its search index with 'cmp [rbp-0x4a8],0xf; jle' at 0x1650-0x1657, but the read path has no equivalent check.

vulnerable_operation.operation: OOB stack read via pointer array dereference + subsequent heap/pointer dereference
vulnerable_operation.address: 0x17e5 (array access) and 0x1844 (pointer dereference in print loop)
vulnerable_operation.expression: hash_array[read_idx] = *(rbp + read_idx*8 - 0x490) where read_idx is attacker-controlled unsigned with no bounds; then *hash_array[read_idx] + [0..31] bytes printed
vulnerable_operation.target: Stack memory beyond hash_array (text buffer, canary, saved rbp, return address) and subsequently whatever address the OOB value points to
vulnerable_operation.size: 8 bytes read from OOB stack slot; 32 bytes read from dereferenced OOB pointer value

impact.reason: At idx 146, the access reads rbp+0x0 (saved rbp), which is a stack address. At idx 145, it reads rbp-0x8 (the stack canary). At idx 147, it reads rbp+0x8 (the return address, a PIE code address). If any of these OOB slots contain a non-NULL value, that value is dereferenced as a pointer and 32 bytes from that target address are printed to stdout. For idx 146 (saved rbp), the value is a stack pointer (0x7ffc...); dereferencing it reads 32 bytes of stack content starting from the caller's frame, leaking stack data. For idx 147 (return address), the value is a PIE .text address; dereferencing it reads 32 bytes of code. The canary at idx 145 is a random 64-bit value; if non-NULL (almost always true), dereferencing it reads 32 bytes from a random address, which may crash or leak data. S1 runtime testing confirmed idx 146 leaks stack addresses (0x7ffc...).

The unsigned index with no upper bound allows reading any 8-byte-aligned stack slot relative to rbp-0x490. For very large indices (e.g., 0xFFFFFFFF), the computed address rbp-0x490+0xFFFFFFFF*8 wraps to a location far beyond mapped memory, causing SIGBUS/SIGSEGV (confirmed by S1 runtime: idx 0xFFFFFFFF causes Bus error, exit code 135). For moderate indices (16-200+), the access reads stack data beyond the hash_array including the text buffer, canary, saved rbp, return address, and caller frame data.

When an OOB slot contains a non-NULL value that is not a valid pointer (e.g., the canary at idx 145 is a random 64-bit value), the subsequent dereference at 0x1844 (movzx eax, BYTE PTR [rax]) will attempt to read from an invalid address, causing SIGSEGV or SIGBUS. S1 confirmed idx 0xFFFFFFFF causes SIGBUS. Additionally, dereferencing the canary value (a random address) at idx 145 would likely crash.

evidence.description: Disassembly shows: 0x17dd: mov eax,[rbp-0x4b0] loads the scanf-read unsigned index; 0x17e3: mov eax,eax zero-extends to 64-bit; 0x17e5: mov rax,[rbp+rax*8-0x490] uses the index directly as an array offset with NO preceding cmp/jcc bounds check. The only check is test rax,rax at 0x17ed (NULL check on the loaded value, not on the index).
scanf format string at 0x21dd is '%u' (confirmed via xxd: bytes 25 75 00 = '%u\0'), reading an unsigned 32-bit integer with no range restriction. The value is stored at rbp-0x4b0.

Stack frame layout confirmed: sub rsp,0x4c0 at 0x1529; hash_array base at rbp-0x490 (flag hash stored at [rbp-0x490] at 0x1587); text_buf at rbp-0x410 (lea rax,[rbp-0x410] at 0x15ce); canary at rbp-0x8 (mov [rbp-0x8],rax at 0x1539). This places: idx 145 = rbp-0x8 (canary), idx 146 = rbp (saved rbp), idx 147 = rbp+0x8 (return address).

Print loop re-reads the OOB slot: 0x182f: mov eax,eax (zero-extend idx); 0x1831: mov rdx,[rbp+rax*8-0x490] (load OOB pointer); 0x1841: add rax,rdx (ptr + loop_offset); 0x1844: movzx eax,BYTE PTR [rax] (dereference OOB pointer value). This dereferences whatever 8-byte value was read from the OOB stack slot, printing 32 bytes from that address.

Contrast with compute path: the compute path bounds its search index with 'cmp [rbp-0x4a8],0xf; jle' at 0x1650-0x1657, limiting to indices 0-15. The read path has no equivalent bounds check, confirming the omission is a bug, not an intentional design choice.

verification_required: Confirm at runtime that idx 145 leaks the stack canary value (8 bytes at rbp-0x8)
Confirm at runtime that idx 147 leaks the return address (PIE base disclosure)
Confirm whether dereferencing the canary value (random address) at idx 145 crashes or leaks data
Determine whether the leaked stack address at idx 146 can be used to defeat ASLR for subsequent exploitation (S3/S4 scope)

vulnerabilities.title: READ_RETURN_VALUE_USED_AS_INDEX_WITHOUT_VALIDATION

root_cause.description: In the compute path of main, the return value of read(0, buf, 0x3ff) is stored at rbp-0x49c and then used to compute an index into the text buffer without checking for error/EOF conditions. At 0x16b7, 'sub eax,0x1' subtracts 1 from the read return value, and at 0x16ba 'cdqe' sign-extends it to 64-bit. If read() returns 0 (EOF) or -1 (error), the computation produces -1 (0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF) or -2 (0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFE) respectively, and the subsequent 'movzx eax, BYTE PTR [rbp+rax*1-0x410]' at 0x16bc accesses text_buf at a massive negative offset, reading far beyond the stack frame boundary.

attack_surface.input: read() return value (affected by stdin EOF or read error)
data_flow: read(0, rbp-0x410, 0x3ff) at 0x16a6 returns number of bytes read (or -1 on error, 0 on EOF)
Return value stored at rbp-0x49c at 0x16ab
mov eax, [rbp-0x49c] at 0x16b1 loads the return value
sub eax, 0x1 at 0x16b7 subtracts 1 (intending to index last byte read for newline check)
movzx eax, BYTE PTR [rbp+rax*1-0x410] at 0x16bc accesses text_buf[ret_val-1]

security_check.expected: The return value of read() should be checked for <= 0 (error or EOF) before using it as an array index. A check like 'cmp eax,0; jle skip_newline_strip' is required.
security_check.actual: No check on the read() return value. The code directly subtracts 1 and uses the result as an index into the text buffer.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Missing validation of read() return value before using it as an array index. If read returns 0 or -1, the index becomes negative (sign-extended to a huge value), causing an OOB read.

vulnerable_operation.operation: OOB stack read via unchecked read() return value used as index
vulnerable_operation.expression: text_buf[read_ret - 1] where read_ret can be 0 (EOF) or -1 (error), producing index -1 or -2
vulnerable_operation.target: Stack memory at rbp-0x410 + (0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF or 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFE) = far below stack frame

impact.reason: If read() returns 0 (EOF, e.g., stdin closed) or -1 (error), the index computation produces a negative value that sign-extends to a huge 64-bit value, and the movzx at 0x16bc reads 1 byte from an address far below the stack frame. This is an OOB read of 1 byte. The read value is only used for a comparison (cmp al, 0xa to check for newline) and is not stored or written anywhere, limiting the impact to a potential crash if the address is unmapped.

If the computed address (rbp-0x410 + 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF = rbp-0x411, which wraps to a very high address) is not mapped, the movzx dereference causes SIGSEGV. This requires the attacker to trigger an EOF or error on read(), which may be achievable by closing stdin or sending specific input.

evidence.description: Disassembly: 0x16a6: call read@plt; 0x16ab: mov [rbp-0x49c],eax (store ret); 0x16b1: mov eax,[rbp-0x49c] (load ret); 0x16b7: sub eax,0x1 (ret-1); 0x16ba: cdqe (sign-extend); 0x16bc: movzx eax,BYTE PTR [rbp+rax*1-0x410] (index into text_buf). No check for ret <= 0 between 0x16ab and 0x16bc.

verification_required: Confirm at runtime that closing stdin (EOF) during the compute path triggers the OOB read or crash
Determine whether the 1-byte OOB read value is used in any subsequent control flow decision beyond the newline comparison

non_vulnerabilities.description: compute_hash256 allocates a 32-byte heap buffer via calloc(0x20,1), initializes SHA256 context, calls SHA256_Update with strlen(text) as length, and SHA256_Final to write the 32-byte digest. The heap buffer is exactly 32 bytes and SHA256_Final writes exactly 32 bytes (SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH). No overflow. Stack canary is present and checked.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: calloc(0x20,1) = 32 bytes; SHA256_Final writes SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH = 32 bytes. Size matches. strlen correctly measures input length for SHA256_Update. No memory safety issue found.

non_vulnerabilities.description: The compute path stores the hash pointer at hash_array[search_idx] where search_idx is bounded by the loop 'cmp [rbp-0x4a8],0xf; jle' at 0x1650-0x1657, limiting to indices 0-15. If idx reaches 16 (all slots full), it prints 'OUT-OF-MEMORY' and continues without storing. The store at 0x16f3 uses movsxd (sign-extend) which is safe for values 0-15.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: The store index is properly bounded by the search loop (0-15). No OOB write possible on the compute path.

non_vulnerabilities.description: read(0, rbp-0x410, 0x3ff) reads at most 1023 bytes into a 1024-byte (0x400) buffer at rbp-0x410. The buffer is 0x400 bytes and read size is 0x3ff, so no overflow. The buffer is memset to 0 before each read (0x15e2 initial, 0x170f per-iteration).
non_vulnerabilities.reason: 0x3ff < 0x400, so the read cannot overflow the text buffer. The buffer is properly sized and zeroed.

non_vulnerabilities.function: main (text buffer zeroing prevents fake pointer planting)
non_vulnerabilities.description: S1 raised uncertainty (U003) about whether user-controlled text buffer content at indices 16-145 could plant fake pointers for the read dereference. Therefore, indices 16-145 always contain zeros (NULL pointers) when the read path executes, and the NULL check at 0x17ed catches them, calling _abort. Fake pointer planting via the text buffer is not possible.

Only the SHA256 hash (not plaintext) is readable via idx 0. The flag plaintext is never stored in memory after hashing. clearenv removes all environment variables including 'flag'.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: The flag is only stored as a SHA256 digest (one-way hash). No plaintext flag is accessible through the read path. clearenv ensures the environment is cleared.

non_vulnerabilities.description: init() calls setvbuf(stdin/stdout/stderr, NULL, _IONBF, 0) and alarm(60). No vulnerability.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: Standard I/O setup and timeout. No security issue.

non_vulnerabilities.reason: printf uses '%s' format with the message argument, not user input as format string. The message is a hardcoded string literal.
